pages.text: After supper, Ayisi sat on the veranda with her grandfather and asked, “Nana, is Ananse real? Is every story true?” Nana Boakye set down his cup. “That is a very good question,” he said.
sentences: After supper, Ayisi sat on the veranda with her grandfather and asked, “Nana, is Ananse real?
Is every story true?” Nana Boakye set down his cup.
“That is a very good question,” he said.
pages.alt: Ayisi with her notebook and pencil sitting beside white-bearded Nana Boakye on a warm lantern-lit Ghanaian veranda at dusk, Nana setting a clay cup on a small wooden table.

pages.text: “Some accounts tell us what really happens in nature,” said Nana. “The Earth spins, so we have day and night. We can test and check that in books and with our own eyes. That is one kind of truth.”
sentences: “Some accounts tell us what really happens in nature,” said Nana.
“The Earth spins, so we have day and night.
We can test and check that in books and with our own eyes.
That is one kind of truth.”
pages.alt: Nana Boakye pointing gently up toward the twilight sky where the first evening stars glow, while Ayisi looks up thoughtfully from the veranda.

pages.text: “Other stories are told to teach us how to live,” Nana continued. “When elders tell of Ananse, we cannot check whether a spider bought the sky god’s stories. Yet the tale teaches us that clever thinking and teamwork matter. That is another kind of truth.”
sentences: “Other stories are told to teach us how to live,” Nana continued.
“When elders tell of Ananse, we cannot check whether a spider bought the sky god’s stories.
Yet the tale teaches us that clever thinking and teamwork matter.
That is another kind of truth.”
pages.alt: Nana Boakye gesturing expressively like a traditional storyteller while Ayisi smiles, imagining a tiny friendly spider web glistening on the veranda rail nearby.

pages.text: “So we must never tell a folktale as if it were a fact we can measure,” said Nana. “And we must never call an old story worthless just because it is a tale. We say clearly what kind of story it is, and we treasure the wisdom it teaches.”
sentences: “So we must never tell a folktale as if it were a fact we can measure,” said Nana.
“And we must never call an old story worthless just because it is a tale.
We say clearly what kind of story it is, and we treasure the wisdom it teaches.”
pages.alt: On the veranda, Nana Boakye holds out both hands evenly like a balanced scale—a closed science book on one side of the low wooden table and a traditional carved wooden drum on the other—while Ayisi watches attentively.

pages.text: Ayisi opened her exercise book and drew two neat columns. On one side, she sketched things we can check: day and night, rain clouds, and bees visiting flowers. On the other side, she sketched stories that teach wisdom: Ananse’s gourd and forest tales.
sentences: Ayisi opened her exercise book and drew two neat columns.
On one side, she sketched things we can check: day and night, rain clouds, and bees visiting flowers.
On the other side, she sketched stories that teach wisdom: Ananse’s gourd and forest tales.
pages.alt: Ayisi leaning over the veranda table drawing tiny simple pictures—a sun, rain cloud, and bee on one side, and a gourd and drum on the other—in her open notebook with a pencil while Nana smiles.

pages.text: Ayisi looked up and smiled. “I can value both,” she said. Nana nodded proudly. “You have understood, my child. Keep asking questions, respect our elders’ tales, and always know which is which.”
sentences: Ayisi looked up and smiled.
“I can value both,” she said.
Nana nodded proudly.
“You have understood, my child.
Keep asking questions, respect our elders’ tales, and always know which is which.”
pages.alt: Ayisi and Nana Boakye smiling warmly together on the peaceful veranda under a deep purple-indigo night sky filled with bright stars.

activities.question: What is the first kind of truth Nana Boakye describes?
options: Facts we can check and observe

activities.question: What does Nana say we should do with folktales we cannot check as facts?
options: Say what kind of story they are and keep their wisdom

items: Some accounts state checkable facts about the world.
Folktales teach wisdom about how to live.
We should state clearly which kind a story is.
We can value both checkable science and wise tales.

glossary.definition: To test or examine something carefully to see whether it is accurate.
Older members of a community respected for their experience and wisdom.
Good judgement and understanding about how to live well.
